title: South Korea's Coinone Warns of Secondary Fraud After Hack of Counseling Vendor Exposes Customer Resident Registration and Bank Account Numbers
text:
South Korea's Coinone Warns of Secondary Fraud After Hack of Counseling Vendor Exposes Customer Resident Registration and Bank Account Numbers — BigGo Finance Ask AI Real-time News Market Earnings Call Event Calendar Watchlist Podcast Market Influencers Earnings Call Event Calendar Watchlist Podcast Market Influencers More Ask AI Real-time News Watchlist Holdings Market Earnings Call Event Calendar Podcast Market Influencers South Korea's Coinone Warns of Secondary Fraud After Hack of Counseling Vendor Exposes Customer Resident Registration and Bank Account Numbers
 Add preferred source Coinone, a South Korean virtual asset exchange, disclosed that the server of its outsourced customer counseling vendor MetaM was hacked, raising the likelihood that personal data of customers with counseling records was leaked. The list of potentially exposed items includes highly sensitive information such as resident registration numbers, bank account numbers and passwords, not just names and contact details. Coinone blocked the attacking IP addresses, strengthened real-time monitoring and switched its customer center to email-based counseling. Member accounts and wallet systems are operated separately from the vendor's servers, and no evidence of direct intrusion into those systems has been confirmed, but the company warned of secondary harm such as voice phishing and identity theft and urged customers to change their passwords. The incident was reported to the Korea Internet & Security Agency, the Personal Information Protection Commission and the Financial Supervisory Service. Key Elements 
 Coinone MetaM Korea Internet & Security Agency Personal Information Protection Commission Financial Supervisory Service Personal Information Protection Act Coinone, a South Korean virtual asset exchange, faces a growing risk of a large-scale leak of customer personal data after the server of an outside vendor handling its customer counseling work was hacked. The exposure goes beyond names and contact details: resident registration numbers, bank account numbers and passwords that customers provided directly during counseling are also on the list of potentially leaked items, raising concerns that the damage could spread to the entire base of customers with counseling records.
 Coinone said on the 15th that it confirmed circumstances in which an external attacker broke into the server of MetaM, its customer counseling contractor, and viewed or extracted counseling information, and that it had notified affected customers. The attacker gained abnormal access to MetaM's server at around 4 a.m. on the 12th, and Coinone learned of the incident after receiving a report from the vendor at around 9:20 a.m. the same day. English-language reports also said Coinone finalized confirmation of the intrusion at around 8 a.m. on the 15th.
 Items confirmed so far as potentially leaked include phone numbers, names, email addresses, dates of birth, bank account numbers, passwords, resident registration numbers, ID document issuance dates, home addresses, virtual asset wallet addresses and transaction identifiers (TXIDs) that customers provided directly during chat or phone counseling. Because the information each customer provided varies by session, however, the actual leaked items may differ from person to person. Coinone plans to let customers check their own leak records directly through separate notices or a personal data leak lookup service. Users with no customer center counseling history are not affected by this incident.
 The company said member accounts and its virtual asset trading and wallet systems are operated separately from the vendor's servers, and that no circumstances of direct intrusion into those systems have been confirmed so far. After learning of the incident, it blocked the IP addresses used in the attack and the access routes to its customer center, and strengthened real-time monitoring of abnormal access and transactions. Operation of the outsourced customer center has been switched to email-based counseling.
 Coinone reported the incident to the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA), the Personal Information Protection Commission and the Financial Supervisory Service, and is investigating the intrusion route and scope of the leak together with the vendor and specialized agencies. It is also directly inspecting the vendor's security management status.
 The company's biggest concern is secondary harm from misuse of the leaked information. It warned customers of the potential for voice phishing, phishing emails, spam text messages and identity theft. In particular, it urged users who provided their passwords during counseling to change not only their Coinone account password but also the passwords of other services where they use the same password. It also advised caution about contacts impersonating Coinone that demand passwords, one-time passwords (OTPs) or verification codes, or that request virtual asset withdrawals or changes to wallet addresses.
 Customers who suffered losses from this incident can claim damages or statutory damages under relevant laws. The customer notice also stated that those who find it difficult to prove actual losses can claim statutory damages of up to 3 million won (approximately $2,200) under the Personal Information Protection Act and other laws.
 Category Details 
 Incident Abnormal access to MetaM server at around 4 a.m. on the 12th 
 Coinone notified Vendor report at around 9:20 a.m. on the 12th 
 Potentially leaked information Name, contact number, email, date of birth, bank account number, password, resident registration number, ID issuance date, address, wallet address, TXID 
 Measures Blocked attacking IP and access routes, strengthened real-time monitoring, switched customer center to email counseling 
 Reporting agencies Korea Internet & Security Agency, Personal Information Protection Commission, Financial Supervisory Service 
 Statutory damages cap Up to 3 million won 
 Note: Leaked items may differ by individual depending on the information provided in each counseling session
 This case illustrates a virtual asset exchange being tripped up by a hole at an outsourced counseling channel rather than in its core security. Exchanges widely use a structure in which customer response is delegated to outside companies, showing that a vendor's security management is directly tied to the exchange's credibility. Industry observers also raise the need to review the practice of having customers directly enter sensitive information such as resident registration numbers and bank account passwords during counseling.
 For investors, the company's explanation that account and wallet systems are separated is not enough for reassurance. Because leaked information can be exploited for identity verification and account access, Coinone users should promptly change their passwords and check for abnormal transaction records. Users of other exchanges would also be safer changing any accounts that share the same password.
